ratings.plot: Based on a true story, primarily on a conflict between two youth gangs, a 14-year-old boy's girlfriend conflicts with the head of one gang for an unclear reason, until finally the conflict comes to a violent climax.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip if you can commit to four hours of Edward Yang's masterwork on the big screen. Metrograph is showing a restored DCP of one of cinema's greatest examinations of adolescent violence and moral drift.

ratings.plot: In Paris outskirts Blanche, a young clerk, befriends Lea, a girl livelier than she is. Lea is going steady with Fabien who is a friend to Alexandre who is going steady with Adrienne but is however loved by Blanche. Somehow a way h...

verdict.reason: Rohmer's late masterpiece about romantic cycles deserves a theater visit—this is the kind of gossamer human comedy that dissolves at home. Metrograph's DCP will preserve the luminous Paris suburbs cinematography that makes the film's emotional arithmetic visible.

ratings.plot: The eldest daughter of a broken and troubled family works to keep the family together and look after her younger siblings, who are slipping into a life of crime.

verdict.reason: A rare New York screening of Hou Hsiao-hsien's essential work on family dissolution and urban struggle. The DCP restoration at Metrograph is the only way to see this 1987 masterpiece theatrically right now.

ratings.plot: Things go wrong for a high ranking mobster when he doesn't follow his boss's orders.

verdict.reason: Kim Jee-woon's control of violence and moral consequence is unmatched in its precision. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes the austere compositions and brutal geometry of the frame sing.

ratings.plot: A young couple leave their mining town home for Taipei where they struggle to eke out a living in an industrial wasteland.

verdict.reason: Hou Hsiao-Hsien's Taipei industrial romance is a masterpiece of patient visual storytelling and the Metrograph DCP restoration makes this the only way to see it. A 1986 film that moves like air and feels like memory.

movies.title: Four Adventures of Reinette and Mirabelle

ratings.plot: Two unlike girls are going to learn each other's world - lovely countryside and bustling Paris.

verdict.reason: A Rohmer film about friendship and class collision belongs on the big screen, and this Metrograph restoration captures the precise social observation that makes his work essential. The four-part structure lets each encounter breathe—the kind of patient filmmaking that demands theatrical attention.

ratings.plot: All the while, Master Chu tries to find his place in the foreign American world.

verdict.reason: Ang Lee's directorial debut deserves a big screen revival at one of the city's best venues. The film's precise balance of humor and tenderness in a cross-cultural family clash plays better theatrically than anywhere else.

ratings.plot: Within the urban gloom of Taipei, four youths face alienation, loneliness, and moments of existential crisis amidst a series of minor crimes.

verdict.reason: Tsai Ming-liang's debut is essential Taiwan cinema and a rare theatrical showing at Metrograph does not come often. Urban alienation has never looked this hypnotic or felt this true.

ratings.plot: Ryuichi Sakamoto's last performance, a concert film featuring just him and his piano playing for the last time before passing away.

verdict.reason: A final document of one of music's great minds at the piano—this is not a concert film you can replace with a recording. Neo Sora captures something sacred in the space between Sakamoto and his instrument that demands the theater's acoustic presence.

movies.title: Zu: Warriors from the Magic Mountain

ratings.plot: A Chinese soldier in an ancient civil war flees the battlefield and gets caught up in a fantastical quest to save the world from evil.

verdict.reason: Hark Tsui's 1983 wuxia-fantasy hybrid is a wild carnival of practical effects and kinetic choreography that demands the big screen. The Metrograph DCP restores the visual madness to its full insane glory.

movies.title: How to Divorce During the War

ratings.plot: Set in Vilnius in 2022, high-flying executive Marija chooses the worst moment to discuss divorce with husband Vytas - one day before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The couple navigates separation amid a refugee crisis.

verdict.reason: A debut feature that finds emotional clarity in catastrophic timing, using a single marriage to frame the chaos of invasion. Blazevicius shoots Vilnius with the precision of a architect documenting a city about to break.

ratings.plot: A live performance of the band Talking Heads shot over the course of three nights at Hollywood's Pantages Theater in December of 1983 and featuring their most memorable songs.

verdict.reason: The greatest concert film ever made—see it on a big screen where Demme's kinetic staging and the band's invention can hit you at full force. Talking Heads at their peak, 88 minutes of pure architectural brilliance in performance.

ratings.plot: When three American doctors-Palestinian, Jewish, and Zoroastrian-enter Gaza to save lives, they find themselves caught between medicine and politics, risking everything to expose the truth.

verdict.reason: A documentary about three doctors working across religious divides in Gaza demands to be seen while the crisis unfolds and the film is in theaters. Poh Si Teng brings journalists' discipline to a story where medicine and witness-bearing become the same act.

ratings.plot: Biopic of 1930s Chinese actress Lingyu Ruan.

verdict.reason: Stanley Kwan's 1991 masterpiece about Lingyu Ruan uses fragmented narrative and layered performance to interrogate cinema, stardom, and historical truth itself. Film Forum's repertory screening of this restored print is essential viewing for anyone serious about film history or the power of biographical cinema.

This is Coppola's definitive cut of a masterwork—see it on 35mm at Film Forum before it leaves. The restoration is the best the film has ever looked in a theater, and the venue's projection will not disappoint.

ratings.plot: An archive-driven exploration of the life, work, and legacy of iconic, pioneering lesbian filmmaker Barbara Hammer.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip to see a major filmmaker's life and work documented with the rigor she deserves. Brydie O'Connor uses archival material to show how Hammer built an entire cinematic language from the ground up, and Film Forum is the right room for it.

ratings.plot: A silent film star falls for a chorus girl just as he and his delusionally jealous screen partner are trying to make the difficult transition to talking pictures in 1920s Hollywood.

verdict.reason: One of the greatest musicals ever made—the dancing is unmatched and the filmmaking is pure joy. Gene Kelly's performance and the iconic title number justify the trip to a big screen.

A rare screening of Bresson's austere masterpiece about interiority and moral collapse—see it on 35mm at Lincoln Center while you can. The restoration reveals the precise geometry of Bresson's compositions and the absolute stillness of his actors' faces.

ratings.plot: American professor John Holden arrives in London for a parapsychology conference, only to find himself investigating the mysterious actions of Devil-worshipper Julian Karswell.

verdict.reason: Tourneur's 1957 masterpiece of atmospheric dread belongs on the big screen where its shadow-work and mounting tension hit hardest. The restoration at Lincoln Center is the place to experience this film's command of mood and its rare balance of supernatural terror and intellectual rigor.

ratings.plot: Misael lives as an independent logger in the woods, enjoying his solitary freedom. When he must care for his older sister, his peaceful existence is upended and the foundations of his carefully constructed life begin to fall apart.

verdict.reason: Lisandro Alonso's new film arrives at Lincoln Center, where a maestro of deliberate landscape cinema deserves a theater and a patient audience. The collision between solitude and obligation—shot in Alonso's glacial, observational style—is the kind of quiet structural work that demands the size and silence of a cinema.

ratings.plot: A glimpse at the lives of two petty criminals in Taipei.

verdict.reason: A rare New York showing of Hou Hsiao-hsien's masterwork on 35mm at Lincoln Center—this is the kind of screening you don't get twice. The camera holds still while Taipei's underworld moves through the frame with the precision of a poet's line break.

ratings.plot: A group of high school students sets off on a school trip to discover the ruins of Pompeii. They are seized by a sense of vertigo. They allow themselves to be overwhelmed by desire and anger, until they surrender completely.

verdict.reason: A rare film about teenage intoxication and desire shot with real formal ambition at one of New York's premier venues. Atlan uses Pompeii's stasis to frame how adolescent bodies move through space and surrender to impulse, and the 16mm cinematography catches light the way memory does.

movies.title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem

ratings.plot: A decade post-death, filmmaker William Greaves reveals his final work: footage of a 1972 gathering he arranged with Harlem Renaissance legends, which he deemed his most significant capture.

verdict.reason: A posthumous William Greaves film showing archival footage of Harlem Renaissance figures from 1972 is a rare historical document that belongs on the big screen. Lincoln Center is the only venue, and this is the kind of cinema history that dissolves into the ether if you skip the theater run.

ratings.plot: A criminal on the run hides in a circus and seeks to possess the daughter of the ringmaster at any cost.

verdict.reason: Browning's strangest masterpiece belongs on the big screen, and Lincoln Center's print restores the full grotesque power of a silent film that still shocks. Lon Chaney's performance—playing an armless criminal who manipulates desire itself—is the kind of physical storytelling that only works in a theater.

ratings.plot: After the success of POINT BLANK and DELIVERANCE, Warner Brothers offered John Boorman the opportunity of a lifetime...the chance to direct a sequel to their smash hit, THE EXORCIST. The result was one of the biggest disasters in ...

verdict.reason: Essential viewing for anyone who cares how great directors fail on studio assignments and what that failure cost them. Kittredge has assembled the definitive account of a legendary misfire, told by Boorman himself and the people who lived through the wreckage.

ratings.plot: A drunken newspaperman is rescued from his alcoholic haze by an heiress whose love sobers him up and encourages him to write a play, but he lapses back into dipsomania.

verdict.reason: Dorothy Arzner's 1932 film about marriage and addiction remains sharp and unsentimental—see it on a big screen before it disappears again. The drunk scenes have a rawness that predates the Production Code's real teeth, and Arzner's direction finds dark comedy in the wreckage.

ratings.plot: A troubled child summons the courage to help a friendly alien escape from Earth and return to his home planet.

verdict.reason: Essential big screen viewing for one of Spielberg's most emotionally direct films. John Williams' soaring theme and the bicycle chase finale demand theatrical sound and scale.

ratings.plot: Soon after a stranger arrives in a little village, a mysterious sickness starts spreading. A policeman, drawn into the incident, is forced to solve the mystery in order to save his daughter...

verdict.reason: Worth the trip for one of the great horror films of the past decade, a film that demands the big screen and repeated viewings. Na Hong-jin's command of suspense, ambiguity, and visual storytelling across 156 minutes is uncompromising, and Metrograph's presentation gives you the image as intended.

movies.title: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp

ratings.plot: A director making a slasher sequel becomes obsessed with casting the original film's 'final girl,' leading both women into psychological and sexual chaos.

verdict.reason: Schoenbrun's follow-up to We're All Going to the World's Fair doubles down on psychological horror and sexual transgression with real formal ambition. The 35mm print at Angelika deserves the big screen.

ratings.plot: A bureaucrat in a dystopic society becomes an enemy of the state as he pursues the woman of his dreams.

verdict.reason: Gilliam's masterpiece of baroque dystopian cinema demands the big screen, and Metrograph's 35mm print restores the intricate production design to full hallucinatory power. At 132 minutes, this is a commitment that pays off—the visual density and structural audacity reward total immersion in a theater.

ratings.plot: Monsieur Hulot curiously wanders around a high-tech Paris, paralleling a trip with a group of American tourists. Meanwhile, a nightclub/restaurant prepares its opening night, but it's still under construction.

verdict.reason: This is one of the great films about modern alienation and you need to see it on 35mm at Metrograph, where the intricate mise-en-scène and geometric comedy actually breathe. Tati built a full city block for this film and shot it in VistaVision; the theatrical frame is not optional.

ratings.plot: A portrait of genius music composer Ryuichi Sakamoto.

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical screening of one of the essential music documentaries of the decade. Schible captures Sakamoto's final creative period with intimate access and formal sophistication that demands a big screen and proper sound.

ratings.plot: Based on Honobu Yonezawa's novel. Set in 16th century Japan, follows Lord Murashige Araki who, besieged in his castle, confronts mysterious crimes and allies with imprisoned strategist Kanbei Kuroda to uncover the truth.

verdict.reason: Kurosawa directing a period mystery with high-stakes psychological intrigue is reason enough to commit. A castle siege built around interrogation and deception plays to his strengths in tension and moral ambiguity.

ratings.plot: In 1951, a group of high schoolers come of age in a bleak, isolated, atrophied North Texas town that is slowly dying, both culturally and economically.

verdict.reason: Watch it; Bogdanovich's black-and-white elegy for small-town America is essential viewing and rarely holds court in theaters anymore. The 35mm print at Nitehawk restores the grain and intimacy that streaming collapses into nothing.

ratings.plot: A counterfeit bill that starts off as a schoolboy prank leads to incarceration and violence.

verdict.reason: Bresson's final film is a masterpiece of moral devastation that demands the theater. The DCP restoration at Metrograph shows the crystalline austerity of his compositions and the accumulating weight of casual cruelty with devastating clarity.

ratings.plot: A poet in love with Death follows his unhappy wife into the underworld.

verdict.reason: Cocteau's masterpiece demands the big screen and the 35mm print at Metrograph restores its dreamlike imagery to full luminosity. A film about desire and loss that only deepens with age.

ratings.plot: After a bad gambling bet, a schoolteacher is marooned in a town full of crazy, drunk, violent men who threaten to make him just as crazy, drunk, and violent.

verdict.reason: One of the great films about masculine violence and social collapse—see it on the big screen while you can. Metrograph is showing a restored DCP of a 1971 masterpiece that demands theater sound and image to land its full nightmare force.

ratings.plot: Portrait of a middle-class family in Taipei. A man in his forties, his teenage daughter and his eight-year-old son experience life, navigating between remorse, hope and disappointment.

verdict.reason: Three hours of Yang's architectural precision and emotional intelligence—one of cinema's great family portraits. The Metrograph screening honors a filmmaker whose work rarely gets theatrical revival.

ratings.plot: In this 19th century, supernatural winter epic, a drunken applejack salesman must go from zero to hero and become North America's greatest fur trapper by defeating hundreds of beavers.

verdict.reason: A genuinely funny action-comedy that earns its theatrical runtime with sustained invention and practical stunt work. Cheslik's commitment to absurdist physical comedy and hand-crafted effects makes this the kind of original film that demands a big screen and a room full of people.

ratings.plot: Acclaimed conductor Thibaut has leukemia and needs a bone marrow donor. Learning he was adopted, he finds an older brother, a musician and factory worker. Their reunion sparks a fraternal, musical journey amidst the town's factory...

verdict.reason: Watch this. Emmanuel Courcol finds genuine warmth in a high-concept premise—a dying conductor and his estranged factory-worker brother bonding through music—and executes it without sentimentality or false notes.

ratings.plot: The aging patriarch of an organized crime dynasty transfers control of his clandestine empire to his reluctant son.

verdict.reason: This is essential cinema, and Film Forum's restoration print is the only reason to see it theatrically tonight. Coppola's control of image, sound, and narrative rhythm demands a big screen and dark room.

ratings.plot: Karsten apparently has it settled. However, in this provincial German town, a moment of weakness turns to disaster, disappointment soon fuels anger, justice hides behind hypocrisy, and evil gradually unfolds.

verdict.reason: A rare North American screening of a masterwork about moral collapse in a small town—see it on a big screen before it disappears. Özge builds dread through ordinary moments and glances, letting hypocrisy and resentment metastasize across an entire community in ways that feel inevitable and chilling.

ratings.plot: Disturbed Blanche DuBois moves in with her sister in New Orleans and is tormented by her brutish brother-in-law while her reality crumbles around her.

verdict.reason: Kazan's masterpiece belongs on the big screen, where the claustrophobia and raw power of the performances actually land. Vivien Leigh's descent into madness is a clinic in acting that demands a theater.

ratings.plot: Fifteen years after murdering his sister on Halloween night 1963, Michael Myers escapes from a mental hospital and returns to the small town of Haddonfield, Illinois, to kill again.

verdict.reason: This is essential viewing on a big screen—Carpenter's control of space, sound, and silence created the template for modern horror and it only works in a theater. The simplicity of the setup and the precision of the execution make it a masterclass in tension that cheap streaming audio will betray.

ratings.plot: An insurance representative is seduced by a dissatisfied housewife into a scheme of insurance fraud and murder that arouses the suspicion of his colleague, a claims investigator.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing for one of the greatest film noirs ever made. Wilder's razor-sharp dialogue and the venetian blind shadows create the template that every crime thriller still follows.

ratings.plot: This Hong Kong-set crime drama follows the lives of a hitman, hoping to get out of the business, and his elusive female partner.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai at peak visual invention deserves the big screen, and this neon-soaked crime film moves with a kinetic energy that streaming kills. Metrograph's DCP presentation restores the chromatic intensity that makes every frame feel like a deliberate painting.

ratings.plot: The early life and career of Vito Corleone in 1920s New York City is portrayed, while his son, Michael, expands and tightens his grip on the family crime syndicate.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip for Coppola's dual narrative at full power on a restored print. Film Forum's restoration brings the 1920s sequences and Michael's consolidation into sharp focus across three hours.

ratings.plot: Odysseus, king of Ithaca, embarks on a perilous journey to return home after the Trojan War.

verdict.reason: Nolan's adaptation justifies the 172-minute runtime and spectacle through scale and technical mastery. Catch the 70mm at Village East by Angelika if you can.

ratings.plot: In the wake of his mother's death and his father's remarriage, a headstrong boy ventures into a dreamlike world shared by the living and the dead in search of his missing stepmother.

verdict.reason: Miyazaki's first feature in a decade is essential theatrical work that demands the big screen. The hand-drawn animation contains visual invention only a master animator can sustain across two hours.

ratings.plot: A story set in the ACME warehouse, the manufacturer of anything and everything used by the Looney Tunes characters.

verdict.reason: Skip the multiplex and catch this at Nitehawk or an Alamo Drafthouse—it's a theatrical comedy that earns the big screen and a crowd. Dave Green built something genuinely funny with real animation craft, and the gags land harder when you're not watching on a phone six months from now.

ratings.plot: Joe and Angela's marriage is on thin ice. When they invite their enigmatic upstairs neighbors for a dinner party, the night spirals into unexpected places.

verdict.reason: Wilde directs a sharp ensemble comedy about marriage and desire with real bite. The 107-minute runtime trusts the material enough to let tension build without padding.

ratings.plot: When a cartoon rabbit is accused of murder, he enlists the help of a burnt out private investigator to prove his innocence.

verdict.reason: Watch it on the big screen—Zemeckis's integration of live action and animation remains a technical marvel that loses its magic on smaller displays. The composite work is intricate enough that theatrical projection reveals details home viewing flattens.

ratings.plot: While a zombie virus breaks out in South Korea, passengers struggle to survive on the train from Seoul to Busan.

verdict.reason: A genuinely propulsive zombie film that uses the train's confined space and forward momentum to generate constant tension. Yeon Sang-ho's control of pacing and character dynamics makes the genre material feel earned rather than obligatory.

ratings.plot: At Westerburg High where cliques rule, jocks dominate and all the popular girls are named Heather, it's going to take a Veronica and mysterious new kid to give teen angst a body count.

verdict.reason: A restored 35mm print of the sharpest teen satire ever made deserves a theater seat and a crowd. Michael Lehmann's direction turns high school nihilism into pitch-black comedy that still lands harder than the original, and the IFC restoration gives the neon-soaked cinematography back its bite.

ratings.plot: Assigned to a county-mandated drug court program, Cody Parsons embarks on the tenuous journey toward recovery amidst the opioid epidemic in rural Ohio.

verdict.reason: A sharp-eyed debut about addiction and survival in rural Ohio that earns its weight through specificity and restraint. Adam Meeks shoots the landscape and the program with equal clarity, letting the place itself become the story.

ratings.plot: Vietnam War's first Black special ops team reunites to share their untold story, revealing hidden military history and exploring whether confronting the past can heal old wounds.

verdict.reason: Watch this. A firsthand account of an erased chapter of military history—the kind of documentary that restores what official channels buried.

This is essential viewing on a theater screen—the animation and sound design create moments of intimacy that demand full immersion. Kyoto Animation's craft in depicting silence and communication through gesture and expression is the kind of work that justifies the ticket.

movies.title: Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown

ratings.plot: A television actress encounters a variety of eccentric characters after embarking on a journey to discover why her lover abruptly left her.

verdict.reason: Essential Almodóvar at peak invention, vital in 35mm. The 88-minute runtime moves like a perfectly wound toy, and Metrograph's print restores the saturated color palette that makes every frame feel like a poster.

ratings.plot: When a menace known as the Joker wreaks havoc and chaos on the people of Gotham, Batman, James Gordon and Harvey Dent must work together to put an end to the madness.

verdict.reason: Watch it. Metrograph is showing the 35mm print, which is the only way to see Nolan's compositions as intended.

ratings.plot: To satisfy his nagging parents, a gay landlord and a female tenant agree to a marriage of convenience, but his parents arrive to visit and things get out of hand.

verdict.reason: Ang Lee's debut remains a perfect balance of comedy and emotional intelligence about identity and family obligation. Metrograph's 35mm print restores the warm, lived-in textures that made this film feel intimate rather than sitcom-bound.

ratings.plot: A paranoid, secretive surveillance expert has a crisis of conscience when he suspects that the couple he is spying on will be murdered.

verdict.reason: One of the essential American films about surveillance, guilt, and moral complicity—see it on 35mm while this restoration plays. Coppola's control of image and sound design creates paranoia that feels immediate and physical in a theater.

ratings.plot: A woman who agrees to a deal to help an old acquaintance. She follows the hero on his adventure and enters dangerous territory where she is then confronted with her own desire.

verdict.reason: Valeska Grisebach's first narrative feature demands a theatrical commitment at nearly three hours, but her control of landscape, tension, and psychological texture justifies the runtime. The film builds moral complexity through patient observation rather than exposition, which only works if you surrender to the screen's scale.

ratings.plot: The Weight, portrays the life of Jung(Cho Jae-Huyn) who grew up as an orphan and was adopted into a family of only a mother and a son. Jung is now a hunchback man due to scoliosis and is a live-in mortician taking care of corpses ...

verdict.reason: A rare screening of a quietly devastating film about dignity and invisible labor that earns its emotional weight without sentimentality. Jeon Kyu-hwan's direction finds grace in the smallest gestures, and the mortuary setting becomes a perfect frame for examining how we honor the forgotten.

ratings.plot: A Manhattan insurance clerk tries to rise in his company by letting its executives use his apartment for trysts, but office politics and his own romantic hopes complicate matters.

verdict.reason: One of the essential American comedies, sharp about ambition and loneliness in a way that still lands. Metrograph's 35mm print restores Wilder's compositions to their full sting.

ratings.plot: On a remote Scottish isle, siblings Isla and Sandy hunt birds and talk to mythical beings while fighting off outsiders. Their lives change when Daniel, an awkward official, arrives to relocate them.

verdict.reason: A debut feature that finds real comedy in isolation, strangeness, and the collision between community myth and bureaucratic intrusion. Louis Paxton's command of tone and landscape—mixing deadpan Scottish humor with genuinely surreal moments—rewards full attention on a theater screen.

ratings.plot: A 19-year-old Anthony Bourdain travels to Provincetown and stumbles into the chaotic world of a restaurant kitchen, setting off a summer that will shape the course of his life.

verdict.reason: Matt Johnson captures a real person before he became legend, finding Bourdain's hunger and recklessness in a kitchen summer that shaped everything after. The film moves with kitchen urgency.

ratings.plot: Woody, Buzz, Jessie and the rest of the gang's jobs are challenged when they're introduced to electronics, a new threat to playtime.

verdict.reason: Pixar's sequels earn their place, and this one reunites the core cast with sharp direction from Stanton. The ScreenX format at Union Square makes the animation design worth seeing larger than life.

ratings.plot: A young woman, studying to be a vet, develops a craving for human flesh.

verdict.reason: Ducournau's debut is a rare horror film that earns its extremity through formal precision and genuine artistic vision. Metrograph's DCP presentation showcases the film's composed cinematography and color work, which are essential to how the body horror lands.

ratings.plot: A psychologist is sent to a station orbiting a distant planet in order to discover what has caused the crew to go insane.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip for one of cinema's greatest meditations on memory and identity, shot with Tarkovsky's hypnotic command of space and time. Metrograph's DCP restoration honors the film's deliberate pacing and architectural cinematography on a proper screen.

ratings.plot: A mermaid princess makes a Faustian bargain in an attempt to become human and win a prince's love.

verdict.reason: The 1989 film holds up—Disney at peak melodic invention—and the 35mm print at Metrograph restores the underwater palette that VHS and streaming flatten. Bring kids or see it alone; either way, catch it in analog.

movies.title: Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie

ratings.plot: New footage by Rushdie's wife shows his recovery path after the attack, capturing both physical healing and renewed hope. Based on his memoir "Knife: Meditations After an Attempted Murder.

verdict.reason: Alex Gibney documents a story of survival and resilience with access that matters—intimate footage from Rushdie's wife showing the aftermath most people never see. This is journalism that only works in a theater, where the weight of testimony demands your full attention.

ratings.plot: Legendary New York poet Ed Saxberger's forgotten works captivate an eccentric group of young creatives, reigniting his artistic passion. Their intrigue intertwines with the bewitching presence of actress Gloria.

verdict.reason: Kent Jones made one of the best films about art and obsession in recent memory, and this 90-minute work about a poet's rediscovery has the focused intensity of a director at his best. Catch it at Film Forum or Lincoln Center before it vanishes — this is exactly the kind of intimate, intelligent cinema those venues exist to champion.

ratings.plot: A lazy, irresponsible young clerk (Sir Tom Courtenay) in provincial Northern England lives in his own fantasy world and makes emotionally immature decisions as he alienates friends and family.

verdict.reason: A foundational British New Wave film that moves with razor wit and genuine melancholy—essential viewing on a big screen. Schlesinger's direction cuts between fantasy and reality with a sharpness that streams cannot match, and Courtenay's performance captures the specific pain of being stuck between adolescence and adulthood.

ratings.plot: A Juilliard-trained violist navigates the New York City freelance classical musician scene, playing gigs that often draw her into the personal lives of strangers, all while living in her oddball family's NYC apartment.

verdict.reason: A sharp, funny film about the precarious life of a working musician in New York that finds real humanity in the gig economy and the people who sustain it. The 78-minute runtime and Hagen's observant direction let the film breathe without overstaying, and the Juilliard violist protagonist grounds the comedy in authentic detail.

ratings.plot: With his debts mounting and angry collectors closing in, a fast-talking New York City jeweler risks everything in hope of staying afloat and alive.

verdict.reason: The Safdie brothers' nerve and craft demand a dark room and loud speakers—the film's manic editing and anxiety are designed for theatrical immersion. The 35mm print at Metrograph adds texture to the neon chaos.

ratings.plot: An undercover cop and a mole in the police attempt to identify each other while infiltrating an Irish gang in South Boston.

verdict.reason: Scorsese at full command of his craft—go for the propulsive screenplay and the ensemble cast firing on all cylinders. The Nitehawk screening gives you a room built for this kind of kinetic crime drama.

ratings.plot: A secret military project endangers Neo-Tokyo when it turns a teenage biker gang member into a rampaging psychic psychopath who can only be stopped by his best friend.

verdict.reason: The 1988 animation remains one of cinema's most kinetic action sequences ever committed to film. See it big.

ratings.plot: Ordinary word processor Paul Hackett experiences the worst night of his life after he agrees to visit Marcy, a Soho resident that he met that evening at a coffee shop.

verdict.reason: Scorsese's funniest film is a masterclass in escalating chaos and one of cinema's great fever dreams about the city turning hostile. The newly restored DCP at Metrograph sharpens the neon-soaked Manhattan nightmare that defined 1980s downtown cool.

ratings.plot: Post-apocalyptic surrealist black comedy about the landlord of an apartment building who occasionally prepares a delicacy for his odd tenants.

verdict.reason: One of the great debut collaborations between Caro and Jeunet—a fully formed vision of grotesque production design and tonal control that rewards the big screen. Metrograph's DCP is the right way to see the intricate set dressing and the film's deliberately artificial color palette.

movies.title: The Night is Short Walk on Girl

ratings.plot: In this comedy about one epic night in Kyoto, a college sophomore goes on a series of surreal encounters with the local nightlife, all the while unaware of the romantic longings of her classmate Senpai.

verdict.reason: Yuasa's direction transforms a single night into a kaleidoscopic fever dream that demands the big screen and full sensory immersion. Metrograph's DCP projection will let you feel the hand-drawn chaos at full intensity.

ratings.plot: An immigrant Romanian family living in Norway is subject to an investigation and faces the scrutiny of the local judicial system.

verdict.reason: Mungiu's portraits of institutional pressure and family fracture demand the theater's unbroken attention. At 146 minutes, this is patient filmmaking about legal machinery grinding against immigrant life—the kind of work that justifies a trip to Lincoln Center.

ratings.plot: A cyborg from the future, identical to the one who failed to kill Sarah Connor, must now protect her ten-year-old son John from an even more advanced and powerful cyborg.

verdict.reason: Cameron's liquid metal effects still hold and the action setpieces have never been matched in the franchise. This is why the Terminator films exist.

ratings.plot: Two melancholic Hong Kong policemen fall in love: one with a mysterious female underworld figure, the other with a beautiful and ethereal waitress at a late-night restaurant he frequents.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-wai's neon-soaked romance is essential cinema on the big screen. Metrograph's DCP presentation brings the saturated colors and kinetic editing to full life.

ratings.plot: Rescued from abandonment and raised by the King and Queen, Oedipus is still haunted by a prophecy--he'll murder his father and marry his mother.

verdict.reason: Pasolini's operatic reimagining of Sophocles is perverse, profound, and rarely screened—the DCP at Metrograph is your chance to experience one of cinema's strangest confrontations with myth and desire. Do not miss it.

ratings.plot: A retelling of the Orpheus and Eurydice myth, set during the time of the Carnaval in Rio de Janeiro.

verdict.reason: The film's color cinematography and Carnaval setting require the 35mm print at Metrograph to sing; it's a sensuous, romantic film that feels authentic to its Brazilian setting in ways no restoration can fully capture at home. Essential repertory.

ratings.plot: Members of a street gang known as the Warriors must fight their way from the Bronx to their home turf on Coney Island when they are falsely accused of assassinating a respected gang leader.

verdict.reason: Walter Hill's street symphony deserves the 35mm restoration at Metrograph, where the cool and the violence sing together. This is why repertory programming exists.

ratings.plot: When the attempt to kill a professor goes wrong, a series of violent events are triggered which force a taxi driver to run for his life.

verdict.reason: Na Hong-jin's kinetic crime thriller justifies the 136-minute runtime with sustained tension and formal control rarely seen in the genre. Metrograph's DCP presentation lets you see every detail of the precise action choreography and nighttime Seoul cinematography.

ratings.plot: When a housewife finds out she is pregnant, she runs out of town looking for freedom to reevaluate her life decisions.

verdict.reason: A restless Coppola film about flight and self-invention, shot on location with real urgency before he became a studio titan. Film Forum is the right place to see a 1969 road movie that refuses easy answers about freedom and obligation.

ratings.plot: Peggy Sue, on the verge of a divorce, faints at her 25th high school reunion, and wakes up to find herself back in 1960, leading her to try to spot and correct the mistakes that led to disappointments and an unhappy marriage.

verdict.reason: Coppola made a genuine time-travel romance that earns its emotional stakes without sentimentality. Film Forum is running it on 35mm, which restores the warmth in Vittorio Storaro's cinematography and makes the 1960s sequences shimmer the way they should.

ratings.plot: Several women enter a science fiction author's life over the course of a few years, after the author has lost the woman he considers his one true love.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai's most visually ambitious film demands a theater screen and Metrograph's DCP restoration lets the neon-soaked production design breathe. The 129-minute runtime tests patience, but the payoff is a rare work of sci-fi romance that uses visual style as narrative itself.

ratings.plot: When a machine that allows therapists to enter their patients' dreams is stolen, all hell breaks loose. Only a young female therapist, Paprika, can stop it.

verdict.reason: See this on 35mm at Metrograph—Kon's dream-logic animation demands the clarity and grain of film stock to land its visual chaos. Ninety minutes of pure invention that justifies the trip.

ratings.plot: When a cable car malfunctions in the mountains, eight people including six students are trapped high above a valley. As time runs out before the final cable fails, rescue teams work against the clock to save the stranded passengers.

verdict.reason: Naqvi brings the precision of a documentarian to real-time rescue drama, turning a mechanical failure into an engine of human endurance. The 98-minute runtime keeps the tension locked tight without padding.

ratings.plot: An American Civil War veteran embarks on a years-long journey to rescue his niece from the Comanches after the rest of his brother's family is massacred in a raid on their Texas farm.

verdict.reason: Ford's masterpiece belongs on the big screen, where Monument Valley and the moral corruption at the film's core hit hardest. Ethan Edwards remains one of cinema's most unsettling protagonists, and the journey from revenge tale to reckoning with racism demands theatrical immersion.

movies.title: Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind

ratings.plot: Warrior and pacifist Princess Nausicaä desperately struggles to prevent two warring nations from destroying themselves and their dying planet.

verdict.reason: Miyazaki's masterwork belongs on the big screen, not at home. The hand-drawn animation and layered world-building demand theatrical immersion.

ratings.plot: A cab driver finds himself the hostage of an engaging contract killer as he makes his rounds from hit to hit during one night in Los Angeles.

verdict.reason: Mann's night-vision Los Angeles is a character unto itself, and the cat-and-mouse dialogue between Cruise and Foxx justifies the theatrical investment. Tom Cruise's silver-haired killer is one of cinema's most magnetic villains, and Mann shoots the city with the precision of a heist film.

Klapisch's 1996 debut is a rare theatrical screening of a film that captures the texture of youth and sibling friction with genuine affection. The 35mm print at Metrograph restores the grainy, lived-in look that defines the film's intimacy.

ratings.plot: An alcoholic man and his two young children barely survive in Taipei. They cross path with a lonely grocery clerk who might help them make a better life.

verdict.reason: Tsai Ming-liang's patient observation of urban poverty demands the big screen and full attention his long takes require. Metrograph's DCP presentation honors the precise compositions that make stillness visible.

ratings.plot: Two pre-adolescent boys both experienced a strange event and later it affects their lives in different ways. One becomes a reckless, sexually adventurous prostitute, while the other retreats into a reclusive fantasy of alien abduc...

verdict.reason: Araki's most disciplined work demands the big screen, and this restoration at IFC Center restores the film's bruised 16mm cinematography to its original clarity. The dual narrative structure—told through fragmented memory and magical thinking—only lands with full force in a theater.

ratings.plot: Twin gynecologists take full advantage of the fact that nobody can tell them apart, until their relationship begins to deteriorate over a woman.

verdict.reason: Cronenberg's most controlled film—a descent into psychological horror built on Jeremy Irons' dual performance and the obsession between two men who share one identity. The IFC Center's 35mm print restores the clinical precision of his direction, where every shot of those customized surgical instruments becomes a weapon against intimacy itself.

ratings.plot: While doing a thesis about violence, Ángela finds a snuff video where a girl is tortured until death. Soon she discovers that the girl was a former student in her faculty...

verdict.reason: Amenábar's debut is a taut thriller that earns its intellectual premise through genuine suspense and formal craft. The film builds dread through meticulous editing and sound design rather than cheap shocks, making this 1996 Spanish landmark worth seeing on a big screen at Lincoln Center.

ratings.plot: Green Beret veteran Rambo takes on a Pacific Northwest sheriff and the National Guard.

verdict.reason: Ted Kotcheff's original is a tight thriller that works as character study, not the dumb action franchise that followed. Stallone gives a genuinely vulnerable performance in a lean 93 minutes.

ratings.plot: The legendary Greek hero leads a team of intrepid adventurers in a perilous quest for the legendary Golden Fleece.

verdict.reason: A masterwork of practical effects cinema that demands the big screen—Metrograph's 35mm print restores Harryhausen's stop-motion sequences to their full compositional glory. The skeleton fight alone justifies the trip.

ratings.plot: Two old pals reunite for a camping trip in Oregon's Cascade Mountains.

verdict.reason: Reichardt's most distilled film—76 minutes of genuine unease beneath stillness—plays differently on 35mm than anywhere else. The print at Metrograph restores the grain and color timing that makes the landscape feel as unsettled as the men walking through it.

ratings.plot: In 1945, immediately following the end of Second World War, a woman who lives with her two photosensitive children on her darkened old family estate in the Channel Islands becomes convinced that the home is haunted.

verdict.reason: Amenábar's 2001 ghost story holds up because it's genuinely unsettling rather than jump-scared, and the twist earns its place rather than cheating the viewer. Metrograph's DCP presentation honors the shadowy cinematography.

ratings.plot: A gay cabaret owner and his drag queen companion agree to put up a false straight front so that their son can introduce them to his fiancée's right-wing, conservative parents.

verdict.reason: Mike Nichols' timing and ensemble work make this comedy land harder on the big screen than it does at home. Nathan Lane and Robin Williams generate real chemistry, and the physical comedy rewards the theatrical format.

ratings.plot: The ethereally beautiful Vicky recalls her romances with Hao Hao and Jack in the neon-lit clubs of Taipei.

verdict.reason: Hou Hsiao-hsien's fluid camera and neon-soaked Taipei nights are essential on the big screen. The DCP restoration at Metrograph brings out the chromatic precision that defines this film's visual language.

ratings.plot: After a car wreck on Mulholland Drive renders a woman amnesiac, she and a Hollywood-hopeful search for clues and answers across Los Angeles in a twisting venture beyond dreams and reality.

verdict.reason: One of Lynch's essential works demands the big screen, and Metrograph's 35mm print restores the nocturnal Los Angeles cinematography to its intended depth. The three-hour runtime rewards full attention in a theater built for immersion.

ratings.plot: The unenviable life of a government-agency clerk takes a horrific turn with the arrival of a new co-worker who is both his exact physical double and his opposite otherwise--he's a confident, charismatic ladies' man.

verdict.reason: Ayoade's formal control and deadpan precision turn a thin premise into a fully realized nightmare—black-and-white compositions and off-kilter sound design make this a film that demands the big screen. Metrograph's DCP presentation honors the visual architecture Ayoade built.

ratings.plot: While preparing for her daughter's wedding in Paris, Gloria remembers the ceremony years before in Guinea-Bissau which consecrated her father as an ancestor.

verdict.reason: A rare Alain Gomis film demands the big screen, and three hours exploring memory, lineage, and ritual across two continents is exactly what cinema does best. Lincoln Center's presentation honors the scope of a work that moves between Paris and Guinea-Bissau with the deliberation of ceremony itself.

ratings.plot: Three company workers who hate their jobs decide to rebel against their greedy boss.

verdict.reason: Mike Judge's corporate satire holds up as a sharp comedy about American workplace culture. Metrograph is screening it on 35mm, the format Judge shot on, and that restoration clarity makes the visual gags land harder than any streaming version.

ratings.plot: A Memphis law school graduate battles an insurance giant.

verdict.reason: Coppola at his most direct and energetic, mining real legal drama from a John Grisham adaptation without the bloat. The 135 minutes moves like a thriller, and Film Forum's print will show you the craftsmanship in every frame.

movies.title: TUCKER: THE MAN AND HIS DREAM

ratings.plot: The story of Preston Tucker, the maverick car designer and his ill-fated challenge to the auto industry with his revolutionary car concept.

verdict.reason: Coppola at full throttle—a visually audacious film about a dreamer destroyed by the machine, shot like a fever dream in Technicolor. Film Forum's 35mm print restores the saturated palette and compositional control that made this a studio-era anomaly in 1988.

ratings.plot: In 1999, a race of she-aliens, the Kilaaks, brainwash Earth's monsters into attacking major cities, prompting a team of astronauts to stop the invaders while the monsters battle Ghidorah.

verdict.reason: The last great Showa-era kaiju spectacle and the most fun monster movie ever made. Honda and Fukuda pack 11 creatures into 88 minutes and let them trash Tokyo with anarchic joy.

ratings.plot: In 1955 New Orleans, small-time private investigator Harry Angel is hired by a man who calls himself Louis Cypher to track down a singer named Johnny Favorite, but the investigation takes an unexpected and somber turn.

verdict.reason: Alan Parker's nastiest work—a descent into corrupt New Orleans that earns every bit of its dread. The film's visual rot and Mickey Rourke's unraveling performance justify the theatrical commitment.

ratings.plot: On a dark, wet night a historic and regal Chinese cinema sees its final film. Together with a small handful of souls they bid "Goodbye, Dragon Inn".

verdict.reason: Tsai Ming-liang's elegiac final night in a movie palace is essential viewing on a theater's big screen. The DCP restoration at Metrograph honors both the filmmaker's precision and the cinema it mourns.

ratings.plot: A rain-soaked couple take refuge in the castle of a transvestite mad scientist from outer space who is about to unveil his greatest creation.

verdict.reason: Essential midnight movie experience that demands the biggest screen and loudest sound system available. The audience participation tradition makes this a fundamentally different film in theaters than at home.

movies.title: Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home

ratings.plot: To save Earth from an alien probe, Admiral James T. Kirk and his fugitive crew go back in time to San Francisco in 1986 to retrieve the only beings who can communicate with it: humpback whales.

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical return for the best Star Trek film—funny, propulsive, and built for the big screen. Nimoy's direction nails the comedy timing and the ensemble chemistry that made this the franchise's breakthrough moment.

ratings.plot: The movie is set in chaotic 1920's China, when warlords fought each other for power while Sun Yat-Sen's underground movement tried to establish a democratic republic. The movie tells the story of three young women and two young me...

verdict.reason: Hark Tsui's 1986 action comedy is a rare theatrical screening of a genuine Hong Kong classic that rewards the big screen. The kinetic staging and inventive action choreography were built for cinema, not streaming.

ratings.plot: A scientist in a surrealist society kidnaps children to steal their dreams, hoping that they slow his aging process.

verdict.reason: This is essential Jeunet and Caro at full visual invention—a rare 35mm restoration at Metrograph that demands the big screen. The production design and practical effects are the whole event; streaming flattens what makes this film worth your time.

movies.title: Star Trek III: The Search for Spock

ratings.plot: Admiral Kirk and his bridge crew risk their careers stealing the decommissioned U.S.S. Enterprise to return to the restricted Genesis Planet to recover Spock's body.

verdict.reason: Nimoy's directorial debut is tight sci-fi adventure that respects the franchise without drowning in nostalgia. The Enterprise theft heist and Genesis Planet mystery move fast enough to justify the theatrical runtime.

ratings.plot: Absent-minded street thug Rusty James struggles to live up to his legendary older brother's reputation, and longs for the days of gang warfare.

verdict.reason: Coppola at his most formally audacious—a 94-minute sprint of black-and-white expressionism that treats a street-gang story like noir fever dream. Film Forum is showing it, which means you get the print quality this precise, image-obsessed film demands.

ratings.plot: Local legend tells of a ship lured on to the rocks of Antonio Bay being enveloped by a supernatural cloud as it sank; the myth says that when this mysterious fog returns, the victims will rise up from the depths seeking vengeance.

verdict.reason: Carpenter at the peak of his craft delivering pure atmospheric dread in 89 taut minutes. The fog itself is the villain, and the photography makes it a character that owns every frame.

ratings.plot: After his quest to retrieve the fabled Golden Fleece, Jason returns to Greece with powerful sorceress Medea. However, when the king banishes her, it's only human that Medea plots her furious revenge. Can they escape her wrath?

verdict.reason: Pasolini's radical reimagining of Greek tragedy demands the big screen—his visual language transforms myth into something ancient and alien. The Metrograph DCP restoration lets you see the bold, deliberate compositions that made this film a rupture in 1969 cinema.

ratings.plot: Confused post-teenage virgin Bernard Chanticleer moves to New York City, falls for cold-hearted inscrutable go-go dancer Barbara Darling, then finds true love with a loyal lass.

verdict.reason: Coppola's debut feature is a scrappy, vital work of sixties vitality that deserves a theater. Film Forum is the only place to catch this restoration on the big screen, and the kinetic direction and New York energy don't survive home viewing.

ratings.plot: In 17th-century France, Father Urbain Grandier's protection of the city of Loudun from the corrupt Cardinal Richelieu is undermined by a sexually repressed nun's accusation of witchcraft.

verdict.reason: Ken Russell's 1971 provocation is a rare restored 35mm screening at IFC Center, and the film's baroque hysteria demands the scale and texture of celluloid. This is the version to see it on.

ratings.plot: Two criminals and their hostages unknowingly seek temporary refuge in a truck stop populated by vampires, with chaotic results.

verdict.reason: Skip the streaming version and catch this genre hybrid on a big screen where Rodriguez's practical effects and tonal whiplash land harder. Nitehawk's midnight-movie atmosphere is the right setting for a film that doesn't take itself seriously but executes its swings with real craft.

ratings.plot: A streetwise young man becomes a bodyguard to score quick cash. He befriends a disillusioned mercenary determined to begin life anew. They find themselves working together to foil an assassination attempt, but their partnership ca...

verdict.reason: Hark Tsui at peak visual invention deserves the big screen, and Metrograph's 35mm print restores the kinetic chaos that makes this film sing. The action editing alone justifies the trip.

ratings.plot: A woman realizes her daughter was born to kill.

verdict.reason: A genuine proto-thriller that invented the blueprint for psychological horror in American cinema, and this restoration plays best on a big screen where the baroque direction and moral dread can breathe. Mervyn LeRoy's command of suspense and the film's refusal to let the audience off easy morally justify the trip to Village East.

ratings.plot: A teacher visits the house of one of his students after the boy goes missing, only to have a horrifying excuse for his absence from school.

verdict.reason: Shimizu's original is leaner and meaner than the remake that followed, and at 70 minutes it hits hard without overstaying its welcome. The theatrical screening at Alamo Drafthouse is the right place to catch this foundational J-horror blueprint on a big screen.

ratings.plot: Hercules must journey into Hades itself to retrieve the magic stone that will free his love from the powers of darkness.

verdict.reason: Mario Bava's color work in this mythological fantasy is extraordinary—the reds and blacks of the underworld sequences justify the trip to Metrograph alone. A rare 35mm print of an Italian genre film that defined its own visual language is essential viewing.

ratings.plot: A love triangle develops between a vampire, her cellist companion, and a gerontologist.

verdict.reason: Tony Scott's feature debut is a visually sumptuous provocation that demands the theater—and this is a 35mm restoration at Metrograph, where the saturated color and precise compositions finally breathe. The film's baroque excess and formal control reward a big screen far more than any home viewing can offer.

ratings.plot: A troubled young man is drawn to a mythical place called Midian where a variety of friendly monsters are hiding from humanity. Meanwhile, a sadistic serial killer is looking for a patsy.

verdict.reason: Barker's visionary creature design and baroque world-building survive the studio butchering, and this 1990 oddity has only grown weirder and more vital in retrospect. The practical effects and practical locations still hold their own on a theater screen.

ratings.plot: Two centuries after her death, a powerful human/alien hybrid clone of Ellen Ripley aids a crew of space pirates in stopping the aliens from reaching Earth.

verdict.reason: Jeunet's visual baroque style transforms a tired franchise premise into something genuinely strange and worth seeing large. The 35mm print at Metrograph is the rare theatrical argument for a film that doesn't hold up nearly as well on smaller screens.

ratings.plot: A recently laid off factory worker kidnaps his former boss' friend's daughter, hoping to use the ransom money to pay for his sister's kidney transplant.

verdict.reason: Park Chan-wook's brutal kidnapping thriller deserves the 35mm print at Metrograph, where the saturated color palette and precise compositions demand the big screen. This is essential for anyone serious about modern genre cinema.

ratings.plot: A newly-possessed high-school cheerleader turns into a succubus who specializes in killing her male classmates. Can her best friend put an end to the horror?

verdict.reason: Kusama's genre instincts have only sharpened since 2009, and this film's blend of teenage friendship and body horror feels prescient now. Metrograph's DCP restoration gives the neon-soaked cinematography the theatrical clarity it deserves.

ratings.plot: An unscrupulous dealer of rare books finds himself at the heart of a string of paranormal events when he is hired to find the last two copies of a text capable of summoning the devil.

verdict.reason: Polanski's baroque mystery thriller rewards patient viewers who surrender to its labyrinthine plotting and occult atmosphere. The 35mm print at Metrograph restores the film's shadowy compositions and makes the baroque production design legible in ways video has never captured.

ratings.plot: After his mother and stepfather have been killed in a barge accident, John Breen is rescued from some East Side toughs by the Lipvitches. He remains in the city, determined to find his real father, who rejected his mother; and aft...

verdict.reason: Allan Dwan's 1927 silent drama has been restored and is screening at Film Forum, a rare chance to see an obscure gem of the silent era in its proper theatrical form. The restoration justifies the trip.

ratings.plot: Berated all his life by those around him, a monk follows his dream and dons a mask to moonlight as a Luchador (Mexican wrestler).

verdict.reason: Jared Hess made something genuinely weird and tender here; Jack Black's commitment to the bit inside that lucha mask is worth the Alamo Drafthouse experience. Few comedies this sincere about passion disguised as silliness.

ratings.plot: A fashion designer must join forces with a C.I.A. agent to combat terrorism.

verdict.reason: Tsui Hark's action filmmaking on 35mm is worth the trip even when the script fails him. The Hong Kong director's visual invention—hyperkinetic editing, impossible physics, genuine stunt work—survives the mess of plot and carries the entire film.

ratings.plot: A slow-burning epic chronicling the emotional journey of four thirty something women in the misty seaside city of Kobe.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip if you can commit to three hours of Hamaguchi's patient, attentive filmmaking about friendship and time. Metrograph's screening rewards the runtime with a proper theatrical space for a film that earns every minute of its duration.

ratings.plot: During a 1937 Shanghai bombing, a soldier and a woman meet under a bridge and promise to reunite post-war. 10 years later, she's a singer who helps a country girl. The girl falls for her upstairs neighbor - the same soldier.

verdict.reason: Hark Tsui's romantic comedy is a rare theatrical outing for a charming 1984 film that deserves the big screen. The Metrograph restoration captures the warmth of his direction and the chemistry between leads in a way streaming cannot match.

ratings.plot: It has been fifteen years since the death of her father, Agamemnon, and Elektra still burns with hatred for Aegisztosz, who conspired with Elektra's mother to kill him.

verdict.reason: Jancsó's formal audacity and political urgency make this a rare chance to see a major Hungarian modernist on the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration renders the director's signature long takes and landscape compositions with the clarity they demand.

ratings.plot: Henri is depressed after losing his job, but finds himself too afraid to go through with suicide. He hires a contract killer to do the job for him instead - but what happens if he changes his mind?

verdict.reason: Kaurismäki's deadpan masterpiece about suicide and inertia deserves a theatrical seat, and Metrograph's restoration makes this the time to catch it. The 79 minutes moves with precision—each silence and awkward pause lands harder on a big screen than it will anywhere else.

ratings.plot: To appease offended gods before going to war, a commander must sacrifice his favorite daughter to them but does so under the pretext of marrying her off.

verdict.reason: Cacoyannis's 1977 adaptation of Euripides deserves the 16mm restoration at Metrograph, a venue built for this kind of classical cinema. The film's stark approach to ancient tragedy plays differently on a big screen than it would anywhere else.

Chantal Akerman's debut is a landmark of feminist cinema and sexual candor that demands the big screen. The 65mm restoration and unbroken takes reveal the formal rigor that makes this film's intimacy so unsettling.

ratings.plot: Members of a music band spending summer in the countryside watch the petty dramas play out among the local folks and among themselves.

verdict.reason: A rare Iosseliani restoration at Metrograph is the kind of programming event that justifies the trip. The director's gift for observational comedy and social texture rewards the 95 minutes on a theater screen where the light and sound matter.

ratings.plot: A swordsmith trains his friend's orphaned son. The boy seeks revenge for his father's murder but loses an arm rescuing the swordsmith's daughter. A hermit girl nurses him, and he learns swordsmanship with his father's broken sword.

verdict.reason: Hark Tsui's kinetic action filmmaking deserves a theater and a restored print. The DCP at Metrograph makes this the rare chance to see a 1995 Hong Kong action film the way it was meant to move.

ratings.plot: Three vignettes from three different directors that tell stories of ordinary people during Taiwan's Cold War period.
ratings.director: Hsiao-Hsien Hou, Chuang-Hsiang Tseng, Jen Wan

verdict.reason: A rare screening of early Hou Hsiao-hsien at a repertory house is always worth the trip. The DCP restoration makes these three portraits of Cold War Taiwan clearer than they've likely been since their original release.

ratings.plot: The year is 1630. A young woman in Laupstad comes to a small mountain village. She witnesses a woman being hunted and captured.

verdict.reason: Anja Breien's 1981 film about persecution in 17th-century Norway is a rare theatrical outing for a director working at the margins of European cinema. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes this austere, difficult work accessible in a way it hasn't been in decades.

movies.title: There Once Was a Singing Blackbird

ratings.plot: A carefree young percussionist roams the streets of Tbilisi, interacting with friends and strangers alike, and tries to avoid responsibilities.

verdict.reason: Iosseliani's debut is a rare chance to see a Georgian master's early work on the big screen. The restoration at Metrograph captures the rhythmic, digressive strangeness that defines his style—a film that moves like conversation and refuses plot convention.

ratings.plot: As the deadline for a historic strike nears, UPS Teamsters across the United States navigate the challenges of building solidarity with their 340,000 co-workers. This film joins UPS workers across the country-a budding UPS driver ...

verdict.reason: Go see it; Yael Bridge's documentary captures labor organizing in real time with urgency and specificity that makes the stakes tangible. The film catches a historic moment while it's still unfolding, and IFC Center is the right room for it.

ratings.plot: An evil force begins to destroy the idyllic paradise of Gandahar, where the citizens are in perfect harmony with nature.

verdict.reason: Laloux's visionary sci-fi animation is too rare and too strange to skip, especially in a restoration. The hand-drawn alien landscapes and philosophical weight demand the big screen.

ratings.plot: N/A

verdict.reason: This is a restored Coppola film at Film Forum—a rare theatrical event that demands the big screen and pristine print. The restoration itself is the draw here; this is how the film was meant to be seen.

ratings.plot: Francis Ford Coppola's "A-side" to his gang war films and S.E. Hinton adaptations (with RUMBLE FISH being the "B-side") remains one of the defining films of an alternate-Brat Pack and '80s masculinity. Starring a veritable who’s who of ‘80s heroes and heartthrobs – Swayze! Cruise! Lowe! Estevez! – in some of the earliest roles of their careers. A teen gang in rural Oklahoma, the Greasers are perpetually at odds with rival group the Socs. When Greasers’ Ponyboy (C. Thomas Howell) and Johnny (Ralph Macchio) get into a brawl that ends in the accidental death of a Socs member, the boys go on the run. Soon, Ponyboy and Johnny, along with the intense Dallas (Matt Dillon) and their other Greaser buddies, must contend with the consequences of their violent lives.

verdict.reason: Coppola's restored cut at Film Forum is a rare chance to see the director's preferred version of an '80s landmark that launched careers. This is an event.

ratings.plot: In Mexico, musician Tere hosts fellow composer Rosa for a TV interview. Their conversation wanders as unexpected guests arrive. A witty, absurdist comedy that lampoons art-world phoniness and pretension while honoring female frien...

verdict.reason: Pereda's deadpan dissection of art-world ego is compact, funny, and honest about how artists actually talk when the stakes are low. At 71 minutes, it respects your time while delivering the precise sting of a master miniaturist.

ratings.plot: A beautiful, superstitious, animal-loving Gypsy is hotly desired by a fox-hunting squire even after she marries a clergyman.
ratings.director: Michael Powell, Emeric Pressburger, Rouben Mamoulian

verdict.reason: Powell and Pressburger's Technicolor melodrama about desire and class collision deserves to be seen restored on a big screen. The film's visual richness and romantic intensity demand the theatrical experience that Lincoln Center provides.

ratings.plot: N/A

verdict.reason: A rare 1986 Hong Kong drama from director Allen Fong deserves the trip to Lincoln Center for this restoration screening. Fong's precise observation of ordinary life and his understated visual style reward the full theatrical commitment.

ratings.plot: Visually structured around four couples making love, one couple at a time; narratively structured around four chapters in lesbian life: older women talking about what it was like in the 30s, 40s and 50s; a look at the hidden eroti...

verdict.reason: Hammer's 67-minute essay on queer desire and historical memory remains radical and necessary work that demands the big screen. The nitrate print restoration at Lincoln Center makes this a rare chance to see a landmark feminist film in the format the director intended.

ratings.plot: Verdi's famous opera is brought to life in this production. The immortal tale of the noble Moor and his beautiful young wife, and of his lieutenant, whose jealousy and lust for power lead him to commit the ultimate treason.

verdict.reason: Zeffirelli's 1986 operatic adaptation demands the theater's sound system and scale—this is not a film to compress at home. Plácido Domingo's Otello and the lush orchestration of Verdi justify the subway ride and ticket price.

ratings.plot: A chambermaid plots to climb the social ladder by marrying a wealthy man.

verdict.reason: A Renoir film of this era demands the big screen, and Lincoln Center's restoration work makes this the right time to see it. The 86-minute runtime is merciful and the chamber drama crackles with his control of ensemble performance and light.

ratings.plot: Exploding out of the AGFA vaults as a brand-new 35mm preservation, this 1990s kung fu fantasia from Hong Kong is a breathtaking combination of action, comedy, and cooking.

verdict.reason: A restored 35mm Hong Kong kung fu film from the 1990s mixing action, comedy, and cooking is exactly the kind of repertory find worth leaving home for. The AGFA preservation and theatrical print make this a one-time screening experience.

ratings.plot: Presented in Japanese with English subtitles Iconic and game-changing, AKIRA is the definitive anime masterpiece! Katsuhiro Otomo's landmark cyberpunk classic obliterated the boundaries of Japanese animation and forced the world to look into the future. AKIRA's arrival shattered traditional thinking, creating space for future generations of ground-breaking movies. July 1988: World War III breaks loose. Then, in 2019 megalopolis Tokyo... As the leader of a group of young, robust delinquents, Kaneda spent his nights tearing through the urban wastes, racing his motorbike against rival groups. One night while riding with his gang, his friend Tetsuo suddenly encounters a strange boy – the product of human experimentation – and is injured in the ensuing crash. Shortly thereafter, a military squadron appears on the scene to take the boy and Tetsuo away to an army research facility. Determined to free Tetsuo from capture, Kaneda sneaks into the army research lab. However, a regimen of extreme experimental procedures has awakened a new power in his friend, and now he is consumed by madness…

verdict.reason: Essential theatrical experience; Ôtomo's 1988 cyberpunk masterpiece demands the big screen and the subtitled original preserves the director's sound design and pacing intact. This is the version that changed animation forever and still looks like the future.

movies.title: Butthole Surfers: The Hole Truth and Nothing Butt

ratings.plot: A documentary feature about the legendary American punk band Butthole Surfers. The film tells the story of how two accounting students from Trinity College in San Antonio found solidarity in their weirdness, recruited like-minded misfits – queers, weirdos, and nonconformists like naked performance artist/dancer Kathleen Lynch – and embarked on one of the most radical rock journeys of all time. Somehow this band, with a defiantly non-commercial name, ended up as a major influence on acts like Nirvana and even scored a No. 1 hit song. Beyond the band’s story, the film tells the human story of the people behind the band. ratings.plot: It is difficult to imagine precisely what cinema would be without its most influential and memorable titles. THE CABINET OF DR. CALIGARI in particular stands out as one such notable title in the international canon that in its time and forever thereafter has been heralded as a masterpiece of its craft, the singular model for expressionist, black-and-white filmmaking. A landmark of horror filmmaking, its visual style is often copied or paid homage, and its remarkable twist ending has become all but a modern trope. Its long, haunting shadows and canted, dreamlike production design stay with viewers weeks, months, and years following an initial viewing. The film is credited for introducing the "twist" ending and inspired EDWARD SCISSORHANDS by Tim Burton, THE IMAGINARIUM OF DR. PARNASSUS by Terry Gilliam, and Martin Scorsese's SHUTTER ISLAND, all of which share many striking similarities to CALIGARI. "The first thing everyone notices and best remembers about THE CABINET OF DR. CALIGARI (1920) is the film's bizarre look. The actors inhabit a jagged landscape of sharp angles and tilted walls and windows, staircases climbing crazy diagonals, trees with spiky leaves, grass that looks like knives. These radical distortions immediately set the film apart from all earlier ones." – Roger Ebert, Chicago Sun-Times

verdict.reason: Watch it. A 1920 expressionist landmark that shaped everything that followed, and live music transforms a silent masterpiece into an event.
